newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Future HK legislature passes residency bill.
newsitem.headline: Future HK legislature passes residency bill.

text.p: The China-appointed legislature that takes over running Hong Kong when it is handed to Beijing passed a crucial bill on Saturday outlining new residency rights for the British colony.

In its last meeting before the July 1 handover, the 60-member provisional legislature set out criteria for permanent residency rights in the territory at the end of Britain's 156 years of colonial rule.
The legislature, sharply criticised by pro-democracy activists, met just across the border in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.
The permanent residency issue is crucial for 750,000 Hong Kong people who have foreign citizenship and want to know if they can keep their "right of abode" status after the handover.

The bill, unveiled by Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa this month, will impose limits on those staying abroad for long periods and tighten rules on immigrants getting permanent residency after July 1.
Some legislators said the bill failed to solve the problem of the immigration of Chinese children into Hong Kong.
Fears of an influx of children from China have escalated in recent months as their number has soared on rumours of an amnesty after the handover.
Many would have permanent residency rights in Hong Kong under a new constitution which grants the right to a Chinese child if, at birth, one parent is a permanent Hong Kong resident.
But such children, which social workers estimate to number 30,000 to 130,000, have to apply for permission before coming -- a process which can take years.
The territory operates a quota system, allowing only 150 mainland Chinese, about 66 of them children, into Hong Kong every day to join their families.
The legislature, which replaces the present fully-elected Legislative Council, also passed three other bills on Saturday.
It took to 13 the total number of bills passed by the interim chamber, including controversial laws that would curb civil liberties.
All of them will be confirmed by another bill set to be passed by the interim assembly in the small hours of July 1, when it formally comes into existence.
The provisional legislature has held its meetings in Shenzhen, instead of Hong Kong, to fend off potential legal attacks, as democrats argue it is illegal for the chamber to operate before July 1.
